# How we are actually building it

## Most of this was written by agents

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/bot-prs-by-month.png){width="100%"}

::: {.attribution}
All of my organisations. Pull requests opened since January 2026, to the
end of July.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
- We have been applying for funding to do this properly. So far without
  success. So we started anyway, at whatever pace we can manage
- **1,143 pull requests** in the EpiAware org from the bot account, all
  time, counted on 10 August. 966 merged, 119 closed unmerged, 58 open
- The same ratio holds across all my organisations, so it is not one
  easy repository
- Median time from open to merge is about four hours, over the 300 most
  recently merged

::: {.callout-important}
Ten times the throughput at ten times the review load is not a win.
:::
:::
::::

## What that buys: a live outbreak model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
- Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. One renewal process, six surveillance
  streams fitted jointly, about 120 refits since May
- Situation reports are French PDFs. Agents read them, and a second pass
  re-scans independently
- The symptom onset curve has no data table, so we recover it from the
  bar chart by pixel colour and axis ticks
- It checks itself against its own past releases, its own past
  forecasts, and two other groups, on every rebuild
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
![](../figures/fig-bvd-model.png){width="100%"}

::: {.attribution}
[BVDOutbreakSize](https://github.com/epiforecasts/BVDOutbreakSize)
(Abbott, Sherratt, Brand, Funk), a re-analysis and extension of McCabe
et al. Diagram from a previous talk.
:::
:::
::::

## What that costs

- Over **30,000 lines** for one outbreak model. 442 commits, 78% from
  agent identities, 10% from Dependabot, 12% typed by a human
- **18% of pull requests closed without merging.** That is the review
  gate working, and it is also the bill
- The full test suite and docs build have hit GitHub's six hour ceiling,
  so the workflow was redesigned around not waiting for it
- The onset digitiser undercounted one situation report by **54%** after
  a change in image compression. A self-check caught it, not a person
- Test coverage is **93.93%**, and the tests were written by the same
  agents that wrote the code. That is evidence the code does what it was
  told to do, not evidence that what it was told was right

## An org agent that runs overnight

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Designed and coded. A GitHub App identity, one fresh container per
  work unit, per-repository one hour tokens, systemd timers on a desktop
- Nightly it would triage issues, draft designs, unstick stalled pull
  requests and open a trickle of small drafts gated on review debt
- It never merges and never approves. That is enforced in the runner,
  not written down in a document
- Design principle one is to assume every prompt injection succeeds and
  make the damage boring anyway
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **The code is written. Turning it on is the part I have not done.**
  And nothing in the org tells a human contributor what any of this
  means for them
- Where do you run a thing like this safely, and who is accountable for
  what it opens?

::: {.attribution}
SciML have been doing the same thing. See "The Agentic AI Maintenance
Bots of the SciML Organization", Rackauckas, earlier this week at this
conference.
:::
:::
